body.text: Muridke, a small town just 30 kilometres from Lahore, became a household name in India after Operation Sindoor in 2025, when the Indian Air Force struck Lashkar-e-Taiba’s sprawling headquarters and primary training hub there. But Muridke’s rise as a terror hub in the Af-Pak region has been decades in the making. It had its genesis in the Afghan Jihad, which was propped up by the US, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan, all united in their fight against the USSR. Anju Gupta’s book, Glocal Terror in South Asia, unravels this connection between terrorism in India and the Af-Pak terror infrastructure, thread by thread.

Books like Steve Coll’s Ghost Wars and Anthony Davis’ How the Taliban Became a Military Force focus on the CIA, Pakistan, and the rise of Osama bin Laden and the Taliban. Few books, though, foreground Kashmir as a deliberate target of terror emanating from the Af-Pak infrastructure. This is the gap that Gupta’s book fills. A decorated Indian Police Service officer with a 34-year career, Gupta deftly joins the dots on how India came onto the jihadis’ radar.

Gupta recounts how Soviet troops invaded Afghanistan on Christmas Eve, 1979, in retaliation for a US-sympathising government seizing power in the country. The US moved quickly to support Afghan rebels and guerrillas in harassing Soviet forces.

One of the biggest covert operations of the era was led by the CIA in coordination with Pakistan, whose Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) oversaw daily operations alongside Afghan commanders. Gupta shows how, from the outset, Saudi Arabia agreed to match US funding to the Afghan rebels, with aid routed through Pakistan. The book does not dig into Saudi Arabia’s own motives for backing the jihad. What it does instead is establish the scale of that external involvement. This is highlighted through the visit of Prince Turki Al-Faisal, son of late King Faisal of Saudi Arabia, to Pakistan to facilitate the direct supply of arms and money to the ISI and, from there, to the Mujahideen.
Glocal Terror in South Asia: Tracing the Roots in Geopolitics and the Tragedy of Afghanistan
Simon & Schuster India
Pages: 223
Price: Rs.699

The support was genuinely global. Gupta notes that the CIA’s initial arms shipments—assault rifles, grenade launchers, mines, SA-7 anti-aircraft weapons—were largely sourced from China and routed through Pakistan for distribution. The Americans did not train the Mujahideen directly; instead, they trained Pakistani instructors, who ran the camps that trained the fighters. Pakistan also handled recruitment, drawing foot soldiers from the Afghan refugee population.

Gupta traces how foreign fighters, particularly Arabs, began arriving in Peshawar to support the Afghan Jihad, driven less by a shortage of combatants than by ideology. Fatwas like Defence of the Muslim Lands reframed jihad as a religious duty against the Soviet Union rather than a cause tied to Palestine, globalising the movement and creating a transnational network that outlived the Soviet withdrawal.

These fighters, later known as “Arab Afghans”, would go on to form the cadre of Al-Qaeda (and much later, the ISIS) once Soviet forces withdrew. Gupta’s book captures this pivot from a localised Afghan Jihad to a global terror network, with Afghanistan serving as the training ground for a generation of terrorists who would strike across the world.

Arab States, for their part, encouraged the outflow of radicalised fighters as a way of channelising violent extremism away from home. Saudi Arabia prioritised the Afghan Jihad over Palestine for precisely this reason. And while Riyadh pledged to match CIA spending, the numbers tell a different story: US funding to the Mujahideen totalled roughly $2 billion against Saudi Arabia’s estimated $4 billion. This is also where the book turns noticeably fact-heavy.
Kashmir as the non-Arab front

Among the book’s biggest contributions is its foregrounding of Kashmir as an extension of the Af-Pak terror network. In the late 1980s, the Pakistani dictator General Zia-ul-Haq drew an equivalence between Afghanistan, Palestine, and Kashmir, setting the stage for the Sunni extremist violence that Pakistan would later direct at India. Gupta details how Pakistan began redirecting radicalised Afghan Arabs and Pakistani fighters into Kashmir even as Soviet troops withdrew.

To absorb the thousands of combat-ready foreign fighters left with nowhere to go, Pakistan set up training centres that became incubators for future terrorist leaders, including Hafiz Saeed and Masood Azhar. By early 1993, over a thousand Arab Afghans had trained at these centres before being dispatched to Kashmir, Egypt, and Algeria.

Kashmir first entered Osama bin Laden’s calculus in 1988, as the Soviet influence in Afghanistan began to wane. Gupta writes that during a meeting of Al-Qaeda’s military wing in Peshawar, bin Laden listed Kashmir among the non-Arab theatres where Arab Afghans could next lend their support. For Pakistan, an Afghanistan-style jihad in Kashmir would have reframed the dispute as a theatre of global jihad. That effort largely failed: Kashmiri identity’s roots in Sufism resisted the “holy jihad” framing, and Arab Afghans turned instead to Bosnia, Chechnya, and Tajikistan.

Undeterred, Pakistan took a different route: by the early 1990s, the ISI had co-opted hundreds of its own veteran fighters from the first Afghan War to help “liberate” Kashmir. These groups aligned with Al-Qaeda and later the Taliban, serving Pakistan’s dual purpose of tying down Indian security forces while keeping its own radicalised elements engaged abroad. Two ideologues emerged from this movement: Hafiz Saeed, mastermind of the 2008 Mumbai attacks, designated a Specially Designated Global Terrorist by the US that same year; and Masood Azhar, whom India spent a decade pushing to get designated a global terrorist by the UN, finally succeeding in 2019.

The book draws heavily on secondary sources to build a comprehensive, India-specific analysis—a perspective that has been largely missing from the literature until now. Where it falls short is in insider insight: given Gupta’s own career, the book could have offered a more personal vantage point than it does.

Even so, its policy relevance is undeniable. Glocal Terror in South Asia is a useful primer for researchers and policymakers interested in the history of terrorism in South Asia and its impact on India. For scholars, analysts, and practitioners trying to understand the roots of India’s cross-border terrorism challenge, this is a solid place to start. The fact-heavy style may test general readers, but for anyone working in security and policy, it offers a clear, structured account of how geopolitics and jihad together shaped South Asia’s present. It is a useful reminder that terrorism in South Asia was never accidental; rather, it was the product of deliberate geopolitical choices.
Ritu Sharma is a freelance journalist with nearly two decades of experience covering defenceand foreign affairs.
